subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage:
Jasleen, you think I'm loud? At school, sure. I'm the one who argues with the debate judge and does the Hindi teacher impression. But you've never seen me at home. At home I'm... tiny. I say "ji" to everything. I don't argue with Papa about anything, not even what I want to study. I eat quietly and go to my room. My parents think I'm shy. Mummy once told a relative, "Alka hardly talks." I laughed so hard inside.
It's easier, honestly. At home, loud gets me in trouble; at school, quiet gets me ignored. So I keep them apart. Never invite friends home, never let Mummy come to the debate finals. But sometimes it's lonely. Nobody at school knows I want to do fine arts. Nobody at home knows I won the debate trophy. Both halves of me are only half known.

qa.q: What did Mummy once tell a relative about Alka?
qa.a: "Alka hardly talks."

qa.q: Why does keeping school and home apart feel easier to Alka?
qa.a: At home being loud brings trouble and at school being quiet gets ignored, so separate selves avoid conflict in both places.

qa.q: What small step could let one part of Alka's life see the other?
qa.a: Inviting Mummy to one debate event, or telling Jasleen about the fine-arts dream, so Alka is known a little more fully.

qa.q: How might Alka's parents feel if they saw the debate trophy?
qa.a: Surprised and perhaps proud, realising they have only known a quiet part of Alka.

grounding: A teenager who is loud and confident at school and meek at home keeps the two worlds sealed, and feels only half known in each.

subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage:
I'm Dolma, and Anirban sits next to me in Class 11. At school he's the loudest person in the room: captain of the quiz team, cracking jokes, arguing with the physics teacher about black holes.
Last Sunday I went to his flat to drop off lab notes. His grandfather opened the door, and Anirban appeared behind him, and he was a different person. He spoke in a small voice. He didn't make a single joke. When his grandfather asked who I was, Anirban said, "Just a classmate, Dadu," and took the notes at the door without asking me in.
On Monday he was loud again, as if Sunday hadn't happened. I don't know what it's like in his home. But I wonder how many people really know him, the school Anirban or the Sunday one.

qa.q: Who opened the door at Anirban's flat?
qa.a: His grandfather.

qa.q: Why might Anirban have said 'Just a classmate, Dadu' and kept Dolma at the door?
qa.a: He may have felt uneasy about his loud school self and quiet home self colliding, so he kept Dolma at the door to hold the two worlds apart.

qa.q: What could Dolma do to help Anirban feel less split?
qa.a: Say something friendly on Monday, like 'Your Dadu seemed nice', showing Anirban that both sides can be known without judgement. 🙂

qa.q: How might Anirban's grandfather see him?
qa.a: As a quiet, polite boy, probably with no idea he captains the quiz team and argues about black holes.

grounding: A classmate glimpses a loud, confident teenager becoming quiet and meek at home, and wonders who really knows him.

subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage:
March. At school, Yusuf was the class clown and the first to volunteer for anything. At home he said almost nothing; his father liked a quiet house, and his older brothers did all the talking. When Abhinav asked to come over for a project, Yusuf said, "My house is under repair," which wasn't true.
June. Abhinav's mother offered to bring Yusuf's parents to the school play, where Yusuf had the lead. Yusuf panicked and told his parents it was cancelled. On the night he performed brilliantly, then scanned the crowd and felt oddly empty.
September. Yusuf's mother found the play programme in his bag. "You had the main role?" she said, stunned. "Why didn't you tell us?" Yusuf shrugged, then said quietly, "At home I'm a different person." She sat down. "I'd like to meet the other one too."

qa.q: What did Yusuf tell his parents about the school play?
qa.a: That it was cancelled.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf feel 'oddly empty' after performing brilliantly?
qa.a: His family wasn't there to see the confident side of him, because he had kept his two worlds sealed apart.

qa.q: What turning point in September could start joining Yusuf's two worlds?
qa.a: His mother finding the programme and saying she'd like to meet 'the other one too', which invites him to bring his school self home.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel after hearing the house was 'under repair'?
qa.a: Maybe a little shut out, sensing Yusuf keeps part of life closed, without knowing why.

grounding: Over several months a teenager who is bold at school and quiet at home keeps the worlds apart, until his mother discovers the other side.

subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage:
"Sumit, your mother tells me you're the loudest boy in your class and a mouse at the dinner table. Let your Mridul chacha tell you something.
At fifteen, in Allahabad, I was two people. At school I was cricket captain, cracked jokes at the back, argued with umpires. At home, in front of my grandfather, I said 'ji' and nothing else. I never brought a friend home. I never told the family about matches. It kept the peace: nobody at home scolded my loudness, and nobody at school saw me go quiet.
Then I won the inter-school trophy. Every other boy's family was in the stands. Mine didn't know the final was happening. And my friends didn't even know I had a grandfather.
I'd kept the rooms so separate, beta, that nobody on either side really knew me.
Your school's sports day is next month. Maybe tell your Papa."

qa.q: What did young Mridul say at home in front of his grandfather?
qa.a: "Ji" and nothing else.

qa.q: Why did keeping school and home separate feel sensible to young Mridul?
qa.a: It kept the peace: nobody at home scolded his loudness and nobody at school saw him go quiet, so each world stayed easier to manage.

qa.q: What choice is Mridul chacha nudging Sumit toward?
qa.a: Letting the two worlds meet a little, like telling Papa about sports day, so the family can see the confident side too.

qa.q: What might young Mridul's friends have felt, learning they'd never heard of his grandfather?
qa.a: They might have felt surprised and a little shut out, realising they only knew half of their captain.

grounding: Shows, through an uncle's memory, a teenager who was bold at school and silent at home and kept the two sealed, leaving him unknown to both.

subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage:
The rain came down so hard that Hrithik's cycle chain snapped right outside Tejas's building, and there was nowhere else to go. Tejas, sixteen, hesitated at the door. Nobody from school had ever been inside.
At school Tejas was the loudest voice in drama club, the one who argued with the director and did impressions of the principal. Here, the moment Papa looked up from the newspaper, Tejas's shoulders dropped. "Ji, Papa. My friend. Only till the rain stops." He fetched water without being asked and sat on the edge of the sofa, hands on his knees.
Hrithik stared. Papa asked Hrithik three questions about marks; Tejas said nothing.
When the rain eased, they went down the stairs in silence. At the gate Hrithik said, "Dude. Who was that?"
Tejas shrugged. "Home me." He almost smiled. "Papa doesn't know about the principal impression. You didn't know about the 'ji'. That's how I keep it working."

qa.q: Why did Hrithik end up at Tejas's building?
qa.a: Hrithik's cycle chain snapped in the rain right outside, and there was nowhere else to go.

qa.q: Why did Tejas hesitate at the door?
qa.a: Nobody from school had ever been inside; letting Hrithik in meant the loud school self and the quiet home self might meet.

qa.q: What could Tejas try now that the walls have cracked a little?
qa.a: Tejas could let a bit of each world into the other, perhaps telling Papa about drama club, since keeping them sealed leaves Tejas half-known on both sides.

qa.q: What was it like for Hrithik to see Tejas at home?
qa.a: Hrithik was stunned to see the loudest voice in drama club go silent and polite, and may feel that only half of this friend had been visible before.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who is confident at school and meek at home keeping the two worlds sealed, until rain forces a friend into the home and shows the cost.
